challenges.name: architecture-data-flow-quiz
challenges.title: Source of truth and the sync/async boundary
challenges.description: Two pieces of the CodeDev architecture proposal: a leaderboard that keeps points only in Redis, and a trace of the new submission flow that answers 202 before grading.

questions.question:
From the architecture proposal, leaderboard section:

  On challenge pass the grader worker runs   ZINCRBY lb:all-time <points> <userId>
  No other table stores points.
  redis.conf:  appendonly yes
               appendfsync everysec
               maxmemory-policy noeviction
  One replica, asynchronous replication, automatic failover.

Statement: "With AOF fsync every second, the sorted set can safely be the source of truth for points, because at most about one second of increments can be lost."
questions.explanation: False. "At most one second" is already acknowledged data that disappears, and nobody can tell which increments were lost, so they cannot be replayed. A failover to the asynchronous replica can lose more than a second. And ZINCRBY is not idempotent: a retried worker job adds the points again, with no record to compare against. Points are facts derived from passed challenges and completed lessons, which live in PostgreSQL; the sorted set should be a projection of them that can be rebuilt (lesson 11) and checked by reconciliation. Redis Patterns covers this mistake in detail. The misconception is that persistence settings turn a cache into a system of record; durability is only one of the properties, the others are an audit trail, idempotent writes and the ability to rebuild.

questions.question:
Trace of POST /submissions in the new design (load test, 340 submissions/s):

  POST /submissions                         38 ms   202 {"submissionId":"sub_81f2","status":"queued"}
    validate + rate limit (Redis)             3 ms
    BEGIN                                     
      INSERT INTO submission (... 'queued')   4 ms
      INSERT INTO outbox (submission.created) 2 ms
    COMMIT                                    9 ms
  (separate trace, linked)  grade sub_81f2   5.2 s   worker grader-7

Statement: "If grader-7 crashes after the API answered 202, the submission is not lost, because the submission row and its outbox row were committed before the API answered."
questions.explanation: True. The API answers 202 only after COMMIT, so the submission and the event that triggers grading are both durable in PostgreSQL, the source of truth. If the worker dies mid-job, the queue redelivers the job after its visibility timeout (or a sweeper re-enqueues submissions still queued after N minutes), and grading runs again; the worker must therefore be idempotent (it writes the result with ON CONFLICT or a status check). This is the point of putting the sync/async boundary right after a durable write: the learner's promise (R6a, accepted before the deadline) is kept even when everything after the boundary fails. The misconception is that asynchronous processing means a crash loses work; it only loses work when the hand-off is not durable.
